dating_note: Wikipedia (Symphonic Dances from West Side Story): scored in 1960 from the 1957 musical, with Sid Ramin and Irwin Kostal preparing the expanded orchestration.

recording.label: Columbia Masterworks
recording.why: Bernstein’s first recording with the New York Philharmonic, which had premiered the suite weeks earlier; sessions at the Manhattan Center in March 1961.

trivia: Bernstein chose nine numbers from his 1957 musical and had them re-orchestrated for a large symphony orchestra, and the first performance was conducted by Lukas Foss rather than by Bernstein. The Mambo is the movement with the shouted "Mambo!" calls.

work: Agnus Dei (choral arrangement of the Adagio)
premiere_or_publication: Barber’s own 1967 arrangement for mixed chorus of the Adagio from his 1936 String Quartet; published by G. Schirmer
dating_note: Wikipedia (Agnus Dei (Barber)): in 1967 Barber set the Latin Agnus Dei text to his Adagio; the Adagio itself dates from 1936 (string-orchestra version sent to Toscanini in January 1938).

recording.label: Hyperion
recording.why: Corydon Singers under Matthew Best, recorded in May 1986 and named by Wikipedia among the recordings of the work; a slow reading of about ten minutes.

trivia: Barber fitted the words of the Agnus Dei to the music of his Adagio for Strings with only small changes, giving the famous elegy a prayer text. The choral version is in B-flat minor and marked molto adagio.

premiere_or_publication: Published and recorded by Vavilov in 1970 on Melodiya, credited to "Anonymous"; world fame after Irina Arkhipova’s 1987 recording (arr. Oleg Yanchenko)
dating_note: Wikipedia (Ave Maria (Vavilov)): composed around 1970 by Vladimir Vavilov (1925–1973), who released it that year ascribed to "Anonymous"; later wrongly credited to Giulio Caccini.

recording.label: Sony Classical
recording.why: Charlotte Church’s 1998 version, arranged by Nick Ingman, one of the recordings that carried the piece worldwide.

trivia: Vavilov, a Russian guitarist and lutenist, published his aria as "Anonymous" on a Melodiya lute record in 1970, and it was later wrongly credited to Giulio Caccini. It reached a worldwide audience after the Soviet Union dissolved, through singers such as Charlotte Church and Andrea Bocelli.

premiere_or_publication: Premiered on 4 April 1977 at the Royan International Festival, with Stefania Woytowicz (soprano) and Ernest Bour conducting.
dating_note: Wikipedia (Symphony No. 3 (Górecki)) says it was composed in Katowice between October and December 1976; the premiere followed on 4 April 1977.

recording.label: Elektra Nonesuch
recording.why: The 1992 Elektra Nonesuch recording with Dawn Upshaw and David Zinman, which sold over a million copies (Wikipedia).

trivia: The second movement sets words scratched on the wall of a Gestapo cell in Zakopane during the war. A 1992 recording with Dawn Upshaw and David Zinman sold over a million copies, far more than a modern symphony normally does.

premiere_or_publication: First performed in Tallinn in 1976, at the concert that introduced the tintinnabuli style, alongside six other works.
dating_note: Dated 1976 by Wikipedia (Für Alina): it was first performed in Tallinn that year, at the concert that unveiled Pärt’s new tintinnabuli style.

recording.label: ECM New Series
recording.why: Alexander Malter’s reading on the ECM album Alina, which takes its title from the piece; recorded in July 1995 and issued in 1999.

trivia: The title echoes Beethoven’s Für Elise, but the dedicatee was the eighteen-year-old daughter of a family friend, who had left for England with her father. Pärt meant the piece as a consolation for her mother, and its two-page score leaves most of the interpretation to the pianist.

dating_note: Wikipedia (Music for 18 Musicians) says Reich composed it between May 1974 and March 1976; it premiered in April 1976, which gives the year used here.

recording.label: ECM Records
recording.why: The first recording, made by Reich and his ensemble and released by ECM in 1978 (Wikipedia).

trivia: The piece rests on eleven chords: each section of about four minutes grows out of one chord and melts into the next, and the last section echoes the first. Reich shaped it over two years in rehearsal with his own ensemble.

premiere_or_publication: First performed in 1979 in Bergen, North Holland, with three pianos and an electric organ; it is usually played today on two or four pianos.
dating_note: Sources disagree, so the range is kept: Wikipedia (Canto Ostinato) says the piece was completed in 1976 and first performed in 1979, while the Dutch Wikipedia article places the writing of the score across 1976 to 1979.

recording.performers: Kees Wieringa and Polo de Haas (two pianos)
recording.label: Emergo Classics
recording.why: The Wieringa and de Haas CD of 1996 received Gold status (over 10,000 copies sold) according to Wikipedia, rare for Dutch contemporary music.

trivia: The score is made of 106 short cells that the players may repeat as often as they like, so no two performances are alike. It is by far Ten Holt’s most played work and has been performed in Dutch railway stations, including Utrecht Centraal in the evening rush hour.

excerpt: Complete piece (about six and a half minutes)
premiere_or_publication: Written in 1977 for string orchestra and a single tubular bell, as an elegy for Benjamin Britten, who died on 4 December 1976.
dating_note: Wikipedia (Cantus in Memoriam Benjamin Britten) dates it to 1977, the year after Britten’s death in December 1976.

recording.label: ECM New Series
recording.why: Recorded in January 1984 by the Staatsorchester Stuttgart under Dennis Russell Davies for ECM’s Tabula Rasa, the same album as the Kremer and Jarrett Fratres.

trivia: The piece begins and ends with silence written into the score, and a bell tolls on the note A at the start and finish. Pärt said he had only just come to appreciate the purity of Britten’s music before his death, and compared it with the ballads of Machaut.

recording.why: The violin-and-piano version of Fratres, played by Gidon Kremer and Keith Jarrett in October 1983 for ECM’s Tabula Rasa (released 1984).

trivia: Fratres (Latin for brothers) has no fixed instrumentation, and Pärt later recast it for violin and piano, cello ensemble, string quartet, an octet of winds and percussion, saxophone quartet and more. It is built as variations on a six-bar theme.

trivia: Jenkins built the work around the 15th-century tune L’homme armé and mixed the Latin Mass with other texts, including the Islamic call to prayer, the Psalms and the Mahabharata. It was commissioned by the Royal Armouries for the Millennium and dedicated to the victims of the Kosovo crisis.

premiere_or_publication: Released on 26 February 2004 on the album The Blue Notebooks (130701, an imprint of FatCat Records).
dating_note: Wikipedia (On the Nature of Daylight) says it was recorded in February 2003 as a protest against the invasion of Iraq; the album carrying it came out in February 2004, a year later.

recording.performers: Max Richter with Natalia Bonner, Louisa Fuller, John Metcalfe, Philip Sheppard and Chris Worsey
recording.why: The original studio version on The Blue Notebooks (130701, 2004) for five strings, recorded in February 2003 per Wikipedia.

trivia: Richter wrote it as part of an anti-war album prompted by the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and it has since become one of the most licensed modern classical pieces. Its use in the film Arrival made that film ineligible for the Oscar for Best Original Score, because pre-existing music was judged too central to it.
